papers.title: Tracing the Roots: A Multi-Agent Framework for Uncovering Data Lineage in Post-Training LLMs
papers.abstract: Post-training data plays a pivotal role in shaping the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs), yet datasets are often treated as isolated artifacts, overlooking the systemic connections that underlie their evolution. To disentangle these complex relationships, we introduce the concept of \textbf{data lineage} to the LLM ecosystem and propose an automated multi-agent framework to reconstruct the evolutionary graph of dataset development. Through large-scale lineage analysis, we characterize domain-specific structural patterns, such as vertical refinement in Math-oriented datasets and horizontal aggregation in General-domain corpora. Moreover, we uncover pervasive systemic issues, including \textit{structural redundancy} induced by implicit dataset intersections and the \textit{propagation of benchmark contamination} along lineage paths. To demonstrate the practical value of lineage analysis for data construction, we leverage the reconstructed lineage graph to create a \textit{lineage-aware diversity-oriented dataset}. By anchoring instruction sampling at upstream leaf sources, this approach mitigates downstream homogenization and hidden redundancy, yielding a more diverse post-training corpus. We further highlight lineage-centric analysis as an efficient and robust topological alternative to sample-level dataset comparison for large-scale data ecosystems. By grounding data construction in explicit lineage structures, our work advances post-training data curation toward a more systematic and controllable paradigm.

summary.takeaway: A multi‑agent framework reconstructs dataset lineage to expose redundancy and guide more diverse post‑training data construction.
summary.problem: Post‑training LLM datasets are treated as isolated artifacts, obscuring systemic connections and hidden redundancy.
summary.method: An automated multi‑agent system builds an evolutionary graph of dataset lineage and samples from upstream leaf sources to create a lineage‑aware dataset.
summary.evidence: Large‑scale lineage analysis reveals domain‑specific structural patterns and a lineage‑aware dataset mitigates downstream homogenization, yielding a more diverse corpus.
summary.limitations: No quantitative evaluation of diversity gains or downstream model performance is provided.
summary.why_for_you: Matches your interest in efficient data selection by exposing redundancy and enabling systematic, diversity‑oriented sampling.

signals.text: Introduces “data lineage” and a multi‑agent framework to reconstruct dataset evolutionary graphs.
Automates lineage graph construction and uses upstream leaf sampling to create a diversity‑oriented dataset.
Analysis uncovers vertical refinement, horizontal aggregation, and redundancy; lineage‑aware sampling reduces homogenization (no quantitative metric reported).

deep_dive.overview: The paper defines data lineage as the systematic relationships among post‑training LLM datasets and proposes an automated multi‑agent framework to reconstruct these relationships into an evolutionary graph. Large‑scale analysis of the graph uncovers domain‑specific structural patterns—vertical refinement in math‑oriented corpora and horizontal aggregation in general‑domain corpora—as well as systemic issues like structural redundancy and benchmark contamination. Leveraging the graph, the authors build a lineage‑aware, diversity‑oriented dataset by anchoring instruction sampling at upstream leaf nodes, which they claim mitigates downstream homogenization and hidden redundancy.

methodology.title: Multi‑Agent Graph Construction
methodology.detail: Agents parse dataset metadata and provenance information to infer parent‑child relationships, iteratively merging edges into a global lineage graph.

methodology.title: Lineage‑Aware Sampling
methodology.detail: Instruction samples are drawn preferentially from leaf nodes (datasets without downstream descendants) to maximize novel content and reduce overlap.

mechanism.title: Evolutionary Graph Representation
mechanism.detail: Datasets are nodes; directed edges encode explicit or implicit derivation links, enabling topological queries about ancestry and redundancy.

mechanism.title: Redundancy Mitigation
mechanism.detail: By identifying intersecting lineage paths, the framework flags structural redundancy and avoids re‑sampling overlapping content.

experiments.title: Large‑Scale Lineage Analysis
experiments.detail: Applied the framework to a broad collection of post‑training corpora, characterizing vertical refinement in math datasets and horizontal aggregation in general‑domain corpora, and detecting benchmark contamination propagation.

experiments.title: Lineage‑Aware Dataset Construction
experiments.detail: Created a diversity‑oriented dataset using leaf‑source sampling; qualitative claim of reduced homogenization and hidden redundancy, without reported quantitative metrics.

findings.title: Domain‑Specific Structural Patterns
findings.detail: Math‑oriented datasets exhibit vertical refinement (nested specialization), while general‑domain corpora show horizontal aggregation (broad merging).

findings.title: Systemic Issues Identified
findings.detail: Structural redundancy arises from implicit dataset intersections; benchmark contamination propagates along lineage edges.

findings.title: Diversity Improvement
findings.detail: Lineage‑aware sampling at upstream leaf sources mitigates downstream homogenization, yielding a more diverse post‑training corpus (qualitative evidence).

contributions: Definition of data lineage for LLM post‑training datasets.
Automated multi‑agent framework to reconstruct dataset evolutionary graphs.
limitations: No quantitative evaluation of diversity gains or downstream model performance.
Reliance on topological analysis without sample‑level validation of content overlap.
Scalability and runtime costs of the multi‑agent reconstruction are not reported.
open_questions: How does lineage‑informed data selection quantitatively affect LLM performance and robustness?
Can the framework handle continuously evolving data streams and incremental updates?
What metrics best capture the diversity improvements claimed by lineage‑aware sampling?

papers.title: Mechanistic Data Attribution: Tracing the Training Origins of Interpretable LLM Units
papers.abstract: While mechanistic interpretability has identified interpretable circuits in large language models (LLMs), their causal origins in training data remain elusive. We introduce *mechanistic data attribution* (MDA), a scalable framework that employs influence functions to trace interpretable units back to specific training samples. Through extensive experiments on the Pythia family, we causally validate that targeted intervention—removing or augmenting a small fraction of high-influence samples—significantly modulates the emergence of interpretable heads, whereas random interventions show no effect. Our analysis reveals that repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) acts as a mechanistic catalyst. Furthermore, we observe that interventions targeting induction head formation induce a concurrent change in the model’s in-context learning (ICL) capability. This provides direct causal evidence for the long-standing hypothesis regarding the functional link between induction heads and ICL. Finally, we propose a mechanistic data augmentation pipeline that consistently accelerates circuit convergence across model scales, providing a principled methodology for steering the developmental trajectories of LLMs.

summary.takeaway: Mechanistic data attribution links specific training data to the formation of interpretable LLM circuits.
summary.problem: Identifying the causal training origins of interpretable units in LLMs is currently unknown.
summary.method: MDA applies influence functions to trace units to samples and intervenes by removing or augmenting high‑influence data.
summary.evidence: Targeted removal/augmentation of a small fraction of high‑influence samples significantly changes interpretable head emergence, unlike random interventions.
summary.limitations: The study reports qualitative effects without quantitative metrics of data fraction or performance impact.
summary.why_for_you: Relevant for data selection research as it offers a principled way to steer circuit development via targeted data.

signals.text: Introduces mechanistic data attribution (MDA) to trace interpretable LLM units to training samples.
Uses influence functions to identify high‑influence samples and performs targeted removal or augmentation.
Shows that removing/augmenting a small fraction of high‑influence samples modulates interpretable head emergence, while random changes do not.

deep_dive.overview: The paper presents Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA), a scalable framework that leverages influence functions to map interpretable circuit components in LLMs back to individual training examples. Experiments on the Pythia model family demonstrate that selectively removing or augmenting a small subset of high‑influence samples markedly alters the emergence of interpretable heads, whereas random edits have no effect. Analysis reveals repetitive structural data (e.g., LaTeX, XML) as a catalyst, and interventions on induction heads concurrently shift in‑context learning ability. A data‑augmentation pipeline is proposed to accelerate circuit convergence across scales.

methodology.title: Influence Function Computation
methodology.detail: Computes the gradient‑based influence of each training sample on a target interpretable unit using standard influence function techniques.

methodology.title: High‑Influence Sample Identification
methodology.detail: Ranks training examples by their computed influence scores and selects the top subset for intervention.

methodology.title: Targeted Data Intervention
methodology.detail: Either removes or augments the selected high‑influence samples and retrains the model to observe causal effects.

mechanism.title: Catalytic Role of Repetitive Structural Data
mechanism.detail: Findings indicate that data with repetitive markup (LaTeX, XML) disproportionately drives the formation of mechanistic circuits.

mechanism.title: Induction Head–ICL Link
mechanism.detail: Intervening on samples that influence induction head formation produces simultaneous changes in the model's in‑context learning performance, providing causal evidence for their functional relationship.

experiments.title: Pythia Family Evaluation
experiments.detail: Applies MDA to multiple Pythia model sizes, comparing targeted high‑influence interventions against random sample modifications.

experiments.title: Metrics of Circuit Emergence
experiments.detail: Measures the presence and strength of interpretable heads and tracks in‑context learning capability after each intervention.

experiments.title: Mechanistic Data Augmentation Pipeline
experiments.detail: Introduces a systematic augmentation strategy that repeatedly injects high‑influence patterns, showing faster convergence of target circuits across scales.

findings.title: Targeted Interventions Modulate Circuits
findings.detail: Removing or augmenting a small fraction of high‑influence samples significantly changes the emergence of interpretable heads, while random changes do not.

findings.title: Structural Data as Catalyst
findings.detail: Repetitive markup data (LaTeX, XML) is identified as a primary driver for mechanistic circuit formation.

findings.title: Induction Heads Affect ICL
findings.detail: Altering induction head formation leads to measurable shifts in in‑context learning ability.

findings.title: Augmentation Accelerates Convergence
findings.detail: The proposed data augmentation pipeline consistently speeds up circuit convergence across different model scales.

contributions: Mechanistic Data Attribution (MDA) framework for tracing LLM units to training samples
Causal validation that high‑influence data drives interpretable head emergence
Mechanistic data augmentation pipeline that accelerates circuit convergence
limitations: No quantitative reporting of the fraction of data altered or its impact on overall model performance
Experiments limited to the Pythia family; generalization to larger or different architectures is untested
Scalability of influence‑function computation for very large datasets is not addressed
open_questions: How does MDA perform on models larger than Pythia and on heterogeneous corpora?
What are optimal criteria for selecting high‑influence samples to balance circuit steering and downstream task performance?
Can the augmentation pipeline be integrated with existing training pipelines without degrading generalization?

papers.title: How Learning Rate Decay Wastes Your Best Data in Curriculum-Based LLM Pretraining
papers.abstract: Due to the scarcity of high-quality data, large language models (LLMs) are often trained on mixtures of data with varying quality levels, even after sophisticated data curation. A natural approach to better leverage high-quality data is curriculum-based pretraining, where the model is trained on data sorted in ascending order of quality as determined by a quality metric. However, prior studies have reported limited improvements from such curriculum-based pretraining strategies. This work identifies a critical factor constraining these methods: the incompatibility between the ascending data quality order and the decaying learning rate (LR) schedule. We find that while curriculum-based training substantially outperforms random shuffling when using a constant LR, its advantage diminishes under standard LR decay schedules. Our experiments show this incompatibility can be mitigated by two simple strategies: (1) employing a more moderate LR decay schedule, where the final LR is only moderately smaller than the peak LR, and (2) replacing LR decay with model averaging, i.e., computing a weighted average of the final few checkpoints. By combining these strategies, we improve the average score on a suite of standard benchmarks by 1.64% over random shuffling, without additional data refinement. Validated on 1.5B-parameter models trained over 30B tokens with various data-quality metrics, our findings call for a re-evaluation of curriculum-based LLM pretraining and underscore the potential of co-designing data curricula with optimization methods.

summary.method: 采用适度的学习率衰减（最终 LR 接近峰值），并用加权检查点平均取代衰减。
summary.takeaway: 当学习率调度与课程共同设计时，基于课程的预训练可恢复 1.64% 的基准提升。
summary.why_for_you: 通过将课程与优化动态对齐，满足您对数据选择和高效训练的兴趣。
summary.problem: 标准的学习率衰减调度与递增数据质量的课程冲突，削弱其收益。
summary.evidence: 在 1.5B 参数模型、30B token 训练下，组合策略使平均基准分提升 1.64%，相较于随机洗牌。

findings.title: Curriculum advantage under constant LR
findings.detail: 在学习率保持不变时，课程排序显著优于随机洗牌。

findings.title: Decay erodes advantage
findings.detail: 标准学习率衰减会消除课程与随机排序之间的性能差距。

findings.title: Combined strategies restore gain
findings.detail: 结合适度衰减和检查点平均可使平均基准分比随机洗牌提升 1.64%。

experiments.title: Training setup
experiments.detail: 使用多种数据质量度量，对 1.5B 参数语言模型在 30B token 上进行训练。

experiments.title: Comparisons
experiments.detail: 在恒定 LR、标准衰减、适度衰减和模型平均下，比较课程排序与随机洗牌。

experiments.title: Evaluation
experiments.detail: 在一套标准语言模型基准上的平均得分。

mechanism.title: Curriculum–LR incompatibility
mechanism.detail: 递增的数据质量将最有信息的样本放在后期训练，而标准衰减会降低后期的学习率，限制其影响。

mechanism.title: Mitigation effect
mechanism.detail: 更平缓的衰减保持后期高质量数据的学习率较高，检查点平均在不再降低 LR 的情况下保留已学知识。

open_questions: 这些策略在更大模型和更长训练时的可扩展性如何？
不同数据质量度量与最佳衰减调度之间的相互作用是什么？
类似的共同设计原则能否惠及其他课程维度，如任务难度或领域多样性？

signals.text: 在共同设计的 LR 调度下，基于课程的预训练比随机洗牌提升 1.64%。
适度 LR 衰减（最终 LR 接近峰值）和检查点平均取代标准衰减。
使用 1.5B 参数模型在 30B token 上训练，在标准基准上测得提升。

contributions: 将学习率衰减识别为限制基于课程的 LLM 预训练的关键因素。
提出两种简易互补策略，使课程排序与优化动态对齐。
实证展示在无需额外数据策划的情况下实现 1.64% 的基准提升。

methodology.title: Moderate LR decay
methodology.detail: 设计一种衰减调度，使最终学习率仅比峰值略低。

methodology.title: Model averaging
methodology.detail: 对最后若干检查点进行加权平均，而非使用衰减学习率。

deep_dive.overview: 本文指出常规的学习率衰减会削弱后期高质量数据的课程训练。恒定学习率下，课程排序优于随机洗牌；但标准衰减会消除此优势。作者提出两项简易改进：更平缓的衰减使最终学习率接近峰值，及用加权平均取代衰减。 在 1.5B 参数、30B token 的实验中，这些调整在标准基准上提升约 1.64%。
